What Is an EventEmitter?

A built-in Node object that lets any number of listeners subscribe to a named event, with no import beyond node:events.

The diagram on the last slide needs something concrete behind that emit('ticket.created', ticket) arrow — some object that a service can call .emit() on, and that every listener can independently call .on() against, without either side knowing the other exists. Node ships exactly that, built in, as EventEmitter:

import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

const bus = new EventEmitter();

bus.on('greeted', (name) => console.log(`Listener A: hello ${name}`));
bus.on('greeted', (name) => console.log(`Listener B: hi there, ${name}`));

bus.emit('greeted', 'Sam');
// Listener A: hello Sam
// Listener B: hi there, Sam

Two things matter here. First, .on(eventName, callback) registers a listener without running it — nothing happens until someone actually calls .emit(). Second, .emit() doesn't care how many listeners are registered for that event name: zero, one, or (as above) several all just get called, in the order they were registered, each with whatever arguments .emit() was given. Nobody calling .emit('greeted', 'Sam') needs to know that two listeners exist, or write either of their names anywhere — this is the same publish/subscribe shape as an event listener in the browser (el.addEventListener('click', ...)), just for events this project defines and fires, not ones the DOM fires for you.

That's the entire mechanism. The only design work left is: one shared EventEmitter instance that every module in this project imports, and an agreed set of event names — both next.
